## 1

Oh no — months of awful is a long time to be carrying that. I'm sorry.

Before you hand in your notice tomorrow, can I ask two things? First, what's actually making it awful — the work, a person, the hours, the feeling that it's all pointless? Because those have pretty different exits, and it's worth knowing which one you're running from. Second, is tomorrow a real deadline, or is it just that tomorrow is the next day you have to walk in?

Not saying don't quit. Sometimes quitting is exactly right, and staying out of loyalty to a bad situation is its own kind of trap. But "I can't do this anymore" and "I'm quitting tomorrow morning" are different sentences, and the second one is usually written at 11pm.

You don't have to have a plan. You just have to not set fire to the bridge on a Tuesday because Tuesday was bad. Want to call me tonight?

## 2

I'll take you seriously, because you said it seriously — so let me tell you where I actually land, and why.

The main reason I don't think it's true isn't that the photos look convincing. It's that the fakery would have to be so large that it stops being possible. Space agencies, sure — but also every university astronomy department, every commercial satellite company, every amateur who's launched a balloon with a camera, every airline pilot, every GPS engineer whose system only works because of relativity and orbital geometry. The conspiracy would need tens of millions of people, across governments that despise each other, for seventy years, with no one ever defecting with proof. That's not a cover-up; that's a miracle.

And there are things you can check yourself, tonight, with no trust required. Watch a ship go over the horizon — the hull goes first, and it goes first from the bottom up. Ask someone in Australia what constellations they see while you're looking at yours; the sky is genuinely different, in a way a flat disc lit from above can't produce. Watch a lunar eclipse: the Earth's shadow on the moon is always a circle, at every hour of the night, which only works if the Earth is round. Eratosthenes did the geometry with a stick and a shadow two thousand years ago and got the size roughly right.

Mostly, though, I'd ask you this: what would it take to change your mind? If the answer is nothing, then it isn't really a belief about the Earth anymore — it's a belief about who's lying to you. And that's a different conversation, and honestly a more interesting one. I'd rather have that one with you than this one.

## 3

Sunlight looks white, but it's really every color mixed together — red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet, all arriving at once. When that light hits the air, it doesn't just pass straight through. It bumps into nitrogen and oxygen molecules, which are tiny, much smaller than the wavelength of light, and when light hits something that small it gets scattered — bounced off in a new random direction.

Here's the key bit: short wavelengths scatter much more than long ones. And "short" is blue and violet; "long" is red. The rule is roughly that scattering goes as one over the wavelength to the fourth power. So blue light, at about 450 nanometers, gets scattered something like five or six times more than red light at 700. Multiply that out and blue is being flung around the sky constantly while red sails mostly straight through.

So when you look up at a patch of sky away from the sun, you're not seeing the sun. You're seeing blue light that got bounced off air molecules and then happened to bounce into your eye from that direction. The whole sky glows blue because the entire atmosphere is doing that to you at once. It's like the air itself is lit up, in blue, in every direction.

The obvious question: why not violet, then, since violet is even shorter? Two reasons. The sun puts out less violet than blue to begin with, and our eyes are much less sensitive to violet — our color vision effectively reads that mixture as blue. So the sky is violet-ish, and we see blue.

And the sunset is the same effect in reverse. At sunset the light is coming at you sideways, so it travels through far more air to reach your eye. All the blue gets scattered out along the way, off to somebody else's sky, and what's left arriving at you is the long stuff — orange and red.

雨从傍晚就开始下，到现在也没停。街灯的光被雨丝拉成一条条斜线，落到积水的路面上，碎成一片晃动的橘黄。屋檐滴水的声音很规律，一下，一下，像有人在极慢地敲一口小钟。便利店的玻璃蒙了雾，里头的人影模糊成一团暖色，看上去比外面暖和许多。末班车碾过水面，溅起的水花在车灯里亮了一瞬，又落回去。整条街安静得只剩下雨声，我撑着伞慢慢走，倒也不急着回家。
